assessments.note: Verified against actual source, not docs: gh api confirms AnswerDotAI/msglm exists (15 stars, last push 2026-04-06). Pulled msglm/core.py directly. _add_cache_control only sets msg['content'][-1]['cache_control']={'type':'ephemeral', ttl?} on whichever content block is last -- never touches the block's text/data payload. The only content mutation is string -> [{'type':'text','text':s}] format normalization, which is byte-identical text in a different envelope (matches the entry's own description). cache_last_ckpt_only calls _remove_cache_ckpts on all messages (pop cache_control if present, same normalization) then re-adds cache_control only to the last message via the same content-preserving function -- exactly 'moves which block carries the marker,' no text side effect. This is a metadata flag on top of Anthropic's own cache_control field, which is itself the established-safe mechanism; nothing here changes what tokens the model reads. Savings correctly left UNQUANTIFIED rather than borrowing Anthropic's headline discount number. None of P1-P5 fit: this isn't a documentation sentence (P1), the key Anthropic uses for cache matching is content-derived, not this wrapper's business (P2 n/a), there's no unenforced caller-side condition inflating the verdict (P3), no hidden intermediary rewrites the request (P4), and there's no price/threshold claim to go stale (P5).

Structural PASS_METADATA argument holds up (content-derived KV-cache reuse, not response substitution; explicit caching adds a reference field, implicit changes nothing on the wire). But the entry's own 'correction' is itself now stale. The entry told downstream customers 'do not repeat 90%,' which may now be exactly backwards. No verifiedAgainst field, no named source, no repo/issue cited at all -- unlike 169/27 this is an unsourced hypothetical, so there was nothing external to spot-check; the flaw is internal. The entry defines the failure window as 'the orchestrator crashes between create() succeeding and the caller durably recording that fact' -- i.e. exactly the case where the durable ledger write never completed. It then claims 'the ledger's job is solely to detect I already did this and return the existing ref with zero additional API calls' -- but if the durable record was never written (per its own premise), the ledger has no ref to return and cannot detect prior success; on restart it would either duplicate-submit (the exact failure it claims to prevent) or need to reconcile against the provider, which requires an extra List/lookup call, not 'zero additional API calls.' The entry's own telemetrySignal section concedes this: certainty 'requires the caller-supplied idempotency key stamped in metadata' -- but the title states Batches.create is non-idempotent (no server-side key to look up by), so that certainty condition isn't actually available. This is a conditional pass whose condition the described mechanism doesn't enforce (P3), compounded by leaning on a caller-supplied/local key for detection without establishing it's reliably content-derived or even durably persisted before the crash (P2-adjacent). PASS_ABSOLUTE requires the wire request to be provably unmodified in the failure case it exists to cover, and here the entry's own stated scenario shows the ledger cannot make that guarantee.

I re-fetched all three of the entry's own cited sources live today (2026-08-18, raw HTML via curl, not markdown) and the mechanism is unchanged:

We automatically pass on cost savings if your request hits caches. There is nothing you need to do in order to enable this." Zero request-shape change, still content-blind-undetectable on the wire — same as the original review found.

2. ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/generate-content/caching (fetched today): explicit caching still works by creating a CachedContent object and referencing it — verbatim from the live REST/SDK samples: `"cachedContent": "'$CACHE_NAME'"` and `cachedContent: cache.name`. 3. Neither caching page contains an output-identity sentence today either (grepped both fetched pages for "identical output/response", "same output", "does not affect" — zero hits), matching the original entry's caveat.

So triage's confirmation that the STRUCTURAL argument holds is right, and my independent re-verification today agrees.

Where triage is also right, and where the entry needs a correction (not a verdict flip): I fetched ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing as raw HTML today (200, 248KB, no cookies/auth wall after a redirect through oauth2authorize/autosignin). Verbatim from the live table: Gemini 2.5 Pro Standard — "Input price ... $1.25, prompts <= 200k tokens" vs "Context caching price ... $0.125, prompts <= 200k tokens" (exactly 90% off); Gemini 2.5 Flash Standard — "$0.30 (text / image / video)" input vs "$0.03 (text / image / video)" caching (also exactly 90% off). Case-insensitive grep across the full page: zero matches for "implicit", one match for "explicit" and it's an unrelated JS feature-flag string (`enable_explicit_template_dependencies`) — there is no implicit/explicit split anywhere on the current pricing page, just one flat "Context caching price" row. I also re-fetched developers.googleblog.com/en/gemini-2-5-models-now-support-implicit-caching/ (200, still live) and it is verbatim unchanged since its `"datePublished": "2025-05-08"`: "We will dynamically pass cost savings back to you, providing the same 75% token discount." Its own internal link to `pricing#gemini-2.5-pro-preview` is now a dead anchor (today's page uses `id="gemini-2.5-pro"`, no `-preview` suffix) — further evidence the post was never revisited after the pricing page was restructured.

So the entry's `savings` field ("Treat the verified rate as 75% ... do not repeat 90%") is now factually backwards against the live source computed straight off the current table, exactly as triage measured. That is a correction to the entry's pricing annotation, which is documentation/marketing content the provider can and does change — CONTRACTUAL_ONLY territory if it were the thing being graded — but it was never what earned this entry PASS_METADATA. The strictVerdict rests on request-shape (implicit = zero change, explicit = reference-field-only), which is unmoved. Recommend updating `savings`/`verifiedAgainst` to the 2026-08-18 figures above (flat 90%, undifferentiated), but the verdict itself stands. Secondary scope note (triage flagged this as secondary too): implicit caching alone would independently qualify for PASS_ABSOLUTE (literally nothing added to the request), but bundling it under the entry's single PASS_METADATA label is the conservative/lower-bound choice for the pair, not an overclaim, so it isn't grounds to overturn either — proposedName above just makes explicit that the discount % is out of scope for what's being verified.

The P1 concern doesn't bite because the structural argument for PASS_ABSOLUTE is definitional, not documentation-sourced, and doesn't run through the contested dollar figures at all.

The entry's reasoning field is: "This is pure post-hoc invoice reconciliation: compare actual per-request logs ... against billed line items, then dispute .... No model request is touched at all." That claim is true by construction of what an after-the-fact invoice audit *is* — comparing logs to a bill and disputing a line item cannot alter what token sequence the model read, which model answered, or how much it thought, because the audit runs after the request already happened. This would hold exactly as well if Vaudit's own case-study numbers were $170 or $17M instead of $1.7M — the mechanism-level verdict isn't a function of the outcome vendor reports.

P1's actual shape is a *documentation sentence standing in for* a structural argument (e.g., a provider saying "we discard the duplicate"). No such sentence is doing that job here. Nobody's word — not Vaudit's, not Anthropic's, not OpenAI's — is what makes "an invoice dispute doesn't touch the wire" true; it's true regardless of what any party asserts. And notably the providers' documentation/statements in this case cut the *other* way (disputing the vendor's claims), so there's no provider assertion propping the pass up even loosely.

The genuinely evidentiary-chain-weak part — the $34M/$1.7M/80% figures, sourced through one financially-interested party (confirmed: Vaudit's own disclosed fee is "1% of bills reviewed plus 30% of refunds recovered," verbatim from my independent re-fetch of the techstartups.com article) relayed via a paywalled Information article, disputed by both named providers — is already where the entry puts it: the "savings" field, which is explicitly a DOWNGRADE with the instruction "do not quote '~5% of spend recoverable' as an expected outcome to a customer." That's the register doing its job correctly, not a gap.

I independently re-fetched the source article rather than trusting the triage's re-fetch, and every quote checks out verbatim, including the ones triage didn't quote (Vaudit's fee structure, the specific denial language from each provider). Nothing found weakens the mechanism claim.

The scope-fit aside — "(not a compute technique)" — is a fair observation but not new: the entry already flags it in its own name, which is the exact remedy this register used for ids 187/220 (push the caveat into the NAME so the pass can't be read wider than it should). No further narrowing is needed; the parenthetical already does that work. I'm not proposing a name change.

Net: the reasoning holds without leaning on any of the contested figures, the contested figures are already correctly quarantined to the (already-hedged) savings field, and independent verification confirms triage's fact-finding was accurate. UPHELD at PASS_ABSOLUTE.

Tag=engineering Current cost: 505.50, Max budget: 500.0"). This isn't the hypothetical "gateways also do routing/caching" caveat the entry's trap text already concedes and waves off as separately-auditable; it's the identity-capture point itself being non-severable from enforcement in the flagship named tool. The condition ("don't let the tag touch enforcement") is a property of which vendor feature you enable, not something the generic mechanism as named enforces — textbook P3, and the register's own stated remedy for this shape (id 187, id 220 precedent, given verbatim in my brief) is to move the condition into the NAME, not leave it in an implementationNote under a generic title. I did not find grounds to fail the entry outright: pure HTTP-header/log capture with zero coupling to any vendor tag-budget/routing/caching feature is still structurally content-blind (headers aren't prompt content, full stop) — so the correct move is the narrower pass the register already prefers over demotion, not FAIL.

refutations.proposedName: Local idempotency ledger dedup for Batches.create retries AFTER the durable success record completes (excludes the crash-before-durable-write race the original entry claimed to solve — that race needs a reconciliation List call the entry says doesn't happen, or it produces the duplicate it claims to prevent)
refutations.reason: Triage's read is correct and the flaw is internal/logical, not a citation dispute, so it doesn't need an external source to settle. Quoting the entry: the failure window is defined as when "the orchestrator crashes between create() succeeding and the caller durably recording that fact" — i.e., exactly the case where no durable write happened. The entry then claims "The ledger's job is solely to detect 'I already did this' and return the existing ref with zero additional API calls." Those two sentences contradict each other: a ledger cannot return a ref it never durably persisted. By the entry's own premise, at restart there is nothing in local storage to detect prior success from, so the mechanism as described has exactly two possible outcomes, neither of which matches the claim — (a) it blindly retries, which IS the duplicate full-batch submission the entry exists to prevent, meaning the model reads a second full batch's worth of tokens, a bar-defined FAIL; or (b) it issues a reconciliation List/lookup call against the provider to check whether the prior create() landed, which is an additional API call the entry explicitly denies ("zero additional API calls") and which the entry never describes as part of the mechanism at all. The telemetrySignal section corroborates this rather than rescuing it: certainty "requires the caller-supplied idempotency key stamped in metadata," but the entry's own title states Batches.create is non-idempotent — no server-side key to look up by — so even the reconciliation path isn't shown to work cheaply. This is P3: the pass depends on the durable record already existing, and that condition is the exact complement of the scenario ("crash-recovery dedup") the entry is named for and built to cover. Unlike a P3 case where narrowing the name into the surviving true case still yields the same interesting claim (ids 187/220), here narrowing to "only when there was no crash" strips out the crash-recovery feature that is the entry's entire reason for existing — what's left is a trivial "don't resubmit if you already have the ref" observation, not the claim that was actually registered. Since the claim as written and named cannot be defended verbatim (per "quote verbatim or do not claim it"), FAIL is the honest verdict for entry id 38 as it stands; a materially different, narrower entry describing only post-success retries (or one that adds and accounts for an explicit reconciliation call) could be re-submitted and evaluated separately.

Tried to refute triage and could not — the contradiction is inside the entry's own two sentences, no external source needed, so the P3 flag holds.

Quote 1 (defines the trigger window): "if the orchestrator crashes between create() succeeding and the caller durably recording that fact, a naive retry would submit a second, full duplicate batch job."

Quote 2 (claims what the ledger does in that same window): "The ledger's job is solely to detect 'I already did this' and return the existing ref with zero additional API calls."

These cannot both be true. Quote 1 stipulates the crash happens *before* the durable record is written. Quote 2 requires that durable record — with the actual returned ref — to already exist so the ledger can hand it back. A ledger entry that was never durably written cannot be read back after restart; there is nothing to detect "I already did this" from. So in the exact window the entry exists to cover, one of two things happens, neither of which is "zero additional API calls, guaranteed dedup": (a) the caller has no record, retries blind, and produces exactly the "pure accidental double-work" the entry claims to prevent — an unauthorized extra request goes out, which is precisely what PASS_ABSOLUTE's "nothing on the wire changed" is supposed to certify doesn't happen; or (b) the caller reconciles against the provider via a List/Get lookup before resubmitting — which is a real, additional API call, contradicting "zero additional API calls" outright.

I checked whether the entry's title itself supports a rescue via server-side idempotency (a retried identical request just getting deduped server-side, which would genuinely satisfy "nothing on the wire changed"). It doesn't — the title is explicit: "Local idempotency ledger over **non-idempotent** Batches.create." No server-side key-matching exists to fall back on, which is exactly why triage's reconciliation-call objection is forced, not optional.

The telemetrySignal section confirms rather than rescues this: it says external certainty "requires the caller-supplied idempotency key stamped in metadata" — but that key only helps if something durable was written *before* the crash and someone then spends a lookup call matching against it. Either way, "zero additional API calls" is false in the scenario the entry is titled around.

Tried the narrowing remedy used at ids 187/220 (move the condition into the name). It doesn't work here: the crash-recovery claim isn't a side clause that can be excised, it's the entire parenthetical in the title — "(crash-recovery dedup)." Strip that out and what remains ("don't retry a call you already know synchronously succeeded") is true but trivial and not distinctively a lever; it wouldn't merit a standalone entry. So this isn't a case for a narrower pass, it's a case where the described mechanism doesn't do what it says in the one scenario that justifies its existence. That's the P3 pattern named in the killer-patterns list almost verbatim ("a conditional pass whose condition the mechanism does not enforce... The register's answer is either to move the condition into the entry's NAME... or to fail it"), and here the name-move option is unavailable, so the remedy is FAIL. No verifiedAgainst field, no external doc to re-check against today's date — the defect is structural/internal, and it survives scrutiny.

refutations.proposedName: Native budget alerts and hard spend caps — Anthropic direct API (org + workspace level); Azure Foundry billing unverified, scope separately
refutations.reason:
Triage's P1 analogy to SQS dedup doesn't transfer, because the thing SQS-dedup is dangerous for cannot happen here. Re-fetched platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits as raw HTML myself today (2026-08-18) and confirm the quote is byte-identical: "Once you reach your tier's spend cap, API usage pauses until the next month unless you request a higher limit." The mechanism has exactly two branches: (1) under cap -- the gate hasn't fired, so the request is provably unmodified without needing to trust any provider claim at all, this is tautological, not documentary; (2) over cap -- "pauses" has no reading under which a completion is delivered. That's the decisive difference from SQS/BullMQ: the P1/P2 danger in those entries is a *delivered, plausible-looking answer* that might silently correspond to the wrong request -- a caller gets an ACK and can't tell if dedup was correct. A spend-capped call produces no ACK, no completion, nothing that could pass as a delivered answer for the bar's actual question ("does the model read different tokens for a request that succeeds"). So even under the triage's worst-case reading -- Anthropic runs inference post-cap and discards it rather than blocking pre-flight -- the customer-observable outcome is identical (no output), which makes the pre/post-inference distinction triage worries about immaterial to the bar, not merely unverified. This is the "structural argument that no request was ever sent" the bar names, applied to "no request was ever answered." I'll concede triage's smaller point: the entry's own reasoning field quotes 'whether the request is sent at all' as if it were the rubric's literal wording -- it isn't; the bar only says "a structural argument that no request was ever sent." That's a sloppy self-citation and should be fixed, but the structural argument survives without that phrase, so it doesn't move the verdict.

Separately, and not raised by triage: the entry lists provider "Microsoft Azure" but verifiedAgainst only the Anthropic-direct docs page, and that page itself contains proof the mechanism is non-uniform across platforms -- a callout reading "Claude Platform on AWS: Spend limits work differently on Claude Platform on AWS." Nothing here verifies Azure's spend-cap mechanism is PASS_ABSOLUTE by the same argument; it's a different, unexamined dependency in the path (the AWS callout is direct evidence the assumption of uniformity is false). Recommend narrowing the entry's name to Anthropic-direct-API scope (the register's established remedy per ids 187/220) rather than demoting the whole entry -- the Anthropic-direct case is soundly PASS_ABSOLUTE and survives the P1 challenge; the Azure claim should be split out and verified against Azure/Foundry's own docs before being folded back in.

Anthropic's docs, "Tool use system prompt" section, verbatim: "When you call the Claude API with the tools parameter, the API constructs a special system prompt from the tool definitions... Here are the functions available in JSONSchema format: {{ TOOL DEFINITIONS IN JSON SCHEMA }}" — this is the exact literal confirmation of the claim triage flagged as unciteable ("Anthropic's own... splices client-supplied JSON schema text into the model-visible prompt"), and it's precisely why the entry excludes tool-schema key order from the safe set. The verifiedAgainst field is empty on the compiled register row, but that's true of 22/69 standing-passes entries (several PASS_ABSOLUTE) — a hygiene gap, not evidence the claim is uncited. Rule 4 (repo/stars) doesn't apply: no repo is cited, only an RFC and a docs page.

Structural (P3): triage's own review concedes the JSON-semantics logic is sound and that the entry correctly excludes array order and tool-schema key order as unresolved. Its remaining objection — that a "not-yet-built" canonicalizer is graded before a live count_tokens experiment — misapplies the P3 caller-condition pattern. The graded claim, as the standing entry itself narrows it ("whitespace between JSON structural tokens, object key order on structural/typed fields, transport framing"), isn't a promise about how some future implementer will behave (like Sidekiq's "keep args small" guidance); it's that JSON structural whitespace and non-duplicate-key object order are destroyed by the parse step that is a bare precondition for the server to use any typed field (you cannot extract temperature as a float without parsing, which discards surrounding whitespace and, for a single key, its position). That's the same class of "structural argument" the bar itself credits for PASS_ABSOLUTE ("no request was ever sent") — no live experiment is needed to establish that parsing precedes use. The entry already self-scopes away from the two hedged items (number-literal/string-escape surface form) and the genuinely open one (tool-schema order), so there's no unenforced boundary left inside the passing claim to fail on.

refutations.proposedName: DynamoDB claim/revert + Bedrock clientRequestToken for exactly-once batch-inference submission under Step Functions at-least-once retry
refutations.reason:
Triage's demotion rests entirely on one claim: that the crash window between "Lambda successfully called Bedrock" and "Lambda durably records that success" is structurally unclosable by DynamoDB-side machinery alone, so a Step Functions retry can legitimately resubmit and cause genuine duplicate inference. That's a real gap in local Lambda/DynamoDB ordering taken in isolation — but it ignores what the receiving API itself does with a duplicate call. I fetched AWS's CreateModelInvocationJob reference (the actual Bedrock batch-inference submission API, matching the entry's own "AWS Bedrock batch inference" provider) as raw HTML, not a markdown summary, and confirmed verbatim: "clientRequestToken: A unique, case-sensitive identifier to ensure that the API request completes no more than one time. If this token matches a previous request, Amazon Bedrock ignores the request, but does not return an error." (docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_CreateModelInvocationJob.html, confirmed against raw source at byte offset ~10534, not just the WebFetch markdown pass.)

That's a provider-enforced, request-level idempotency guarantee sitting exactly at the point the triage says is unguarded. A "claim/revert state machine for exactly-once batch orchestration" against this specific API would derive clientRequestToken deterministically from the same record-identity key already used for the DynamoDB conditional-write claim — that's the API's documented, purpose-built use case, not an arbitrary implementation choice. So even in the crash window triage identifies (submit succeeds, Lambda dies before recording, Step Functions retries, DynamoDB shows unclaimed/reverted, Lambda resubmits): Bedrock sees the repeated token and ignores the second call. No second job is created, no additional prompts are read, no additional inference happens. The specific failure mode triage built the demotion on — "a different amount of inference work happens" — doesn't occur, because the provider's own contract prevents it, not a heuristic time margin.

This is why P3 doesn't apply here the way it did at id 220/187: those conditions were properties of the CALLER (job idempotency, full-request hashing) that the mechanism itself did nothing to enforce. Here the closing condition is a property of the PROVIDER'S API contract — unconditional, documented, and independent of the customer's own timing margins. The entry's "deadline guard" line is a belt-and-suspenders addition on top of this, not the sole defense triage treated it as.

I'm not fully certifying the specific unnamed practitioner doc actually wired clientRequestToken through (that detail isn't in the entry text, and per the no-citable-source complaint, there's no repo to check under rule 4 — this is generic AWS-service plumbing, not a named tool). That residual uncertainty is real, which is why I'm proposing the register's established remedy (ids 187, 220): anchor the enforcing mechanism in the entry NAME rather than leave it to be read as "DynamoDB ordering alone solves this," which is the reading triage correctly showed doesn't hold on its own. With the name narrowed to name the actual closing mechanism, PASS_ABSOLUTE stands — the "verifiedAgainst: not re-verified" field should be updated to cite the AWS doc above rather than "accepted as internally consistent."

refutations.proposedName: Conditional-write claim/revert for Bedrock batch orchestration — narrows duplicate-submission risk, does not provably eliminate it (unverified practitioner narrative, no named source)
refutations.reason:
I tried to rescue PASS_ABSOLUTE and could not, for a reason that goes beyond triage's own argument.

First, the disqualifier triage already named is real: rule 5 is "quote verbatim or do not claim it," and this entry has nothing to quote. provenance is "practitioner-data" naming no repo/doc/URL; verifiedAgainst literally says "not re-verified — accepted as... internally-consistent"; savings is "UNQUANTIFIED"; telemetrySignal is "Not detectable from our side at all." Per rule 4 I looked for a load-bearing repo/tool to check stars and last-push and there is none named — there is nothing in this entry that is checkable against a source, which is the one move ("YOUR LENS") I was asked to make. That alone means PASS_ABSOLUTE can only rest on "a structural argument that no request was ever sent" (the bar's own second path), not on a measurement, since no measurement exists.

Second, I went and checked whether that structural argument is actually watertight, using AWS's own current docs (fetched today, 2026-08-18) rather than reasoning in the abstract. Bedrock's CreateModelInvocationJob API — the exact call this entry's whole mechanism exists to protect — has a native idempotency parameter:

"clientRequestToken — A unique, case-sensitive identifier to ensure that the API request completes no more than one time. If this token matches a previous request, Amazon Bedrock ignores the request, but does not return an error."
(https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_CreateModelInvocationJob.html, Required: No)

This is exactly the mechanism that would close the crash window triage identified — Lambda submits successfully, gets SIGKILLed before durably recording that fact, Step Functions retries into a reverted/unclaimed record and resubmits. If the resubmission carries the same clientRequestToken as the original (e.g., derived from the batch record's own key), Bedrock itself dedupes it server-side and no second inference job runs, structurally, provider-guaranteed.

But the entry never mentions this token. Its described mechanism is DynamoDB conditional writes + Step Functions retry semantics + "Lambda SIGKILL deadline guards" — nothing about tying the actual Bedrock call to a stable, content-derived idempotency token. A time-budget deadline guard and a clientRequestToken solve different problems: the guard reduces how often the race window is entered, the token is what would make entering it harmless. Without confirmation the design uses the token, the gap triage described is real and, as literally described, unclosed — that's the P3 pattern exactly (the closing condition is a property of a specific unstated implementation choice, not something DynamoDB's atomicity or the deadline guard gives for free).

Where I land differently from triage: I don't think this is confidently a FAIL, because I can't rule out that the actual (unnamed) implementation does pass a stable clientRequestToken — it's the standard, AWS-documented pattern for precisely this failure mode, and a practitioner sophisticated enough to build a claim/revert state machine with deadline guards would plausibly know about it. We simply aren't told either way, and there's no source to check. That combination — a real, un-ruled-out gap, zero named source, zero measurement, and a rescuing mechanism that may or may not be in use — is "could not be settled," not "confirmed broken." I'm overturning PASS_ABSOLUTE to INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than to FAIL or CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (there's no provider documentation sentence being relied on here — the claim is customer narrative, not AWS's word — so CONTRACTUAL_ONLY's "provider asserts identity" doesn't fit either).

That is a structural argument against the pass, not merely a documentation sentence (P1) and not merely an unquantified doubt (INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE) — the telemetrySignal as written is demonstrably unable to separate the two populations, so PASS_ABSOLUTE cannot stand as an unscoped claim.

Unlike ids 187/220, I don't see a rescuing narrower name: the underlying condition ("nobody, ever, reads this") is not something any request-side signal can establish — proving a negative over an unbounded future horizon — so there is no scoped version of "confirmed via telemetry" that survives. A genuinely defensible version would have to drop telemetry-based detection entirely and substitute an out-of-band administrative fact (e.g., key tied to a decommissioned project/terminated team in the billing system), which is a different mechanism than the one this entry describes. refutations.proposedName: Automatic caching, provider-managed breakpoint/routing — split by provider: Anthropic (single top-level cache_control auto-placed at last cacheable block, sliding forward each turn) vs. OpenAI (zero-parameter longest-prefix routing via prompt_cache_key hash; no cache_control field exists)
refutations.reason: Triage's facts are correct but its conclusion overshoots into a demotion the mechanism doesn't support. Verified live: Anthropic docs confirm "the system automatically applies the cache breakpoint to the last cacheable block and moves it forward as conversations grow" — exactly what the entry claims. OpenAI docs confirm "Prompt Caching works automatically for eligible requests, with no code changes required" via "a hash of the initial prefix of the prompt" — no cache_control parameter exists there, so the entry's single telemetrySignal sentence is genuinely inapplicable to one of its two named providers, and the primary-doc label with zero quotes/no verifiedAgainst is a real citation defect. But the bar only asks whether the model reads different tokens, a different model answers, or a different amount of thinking happens. Under Anthropic's own request schema, cache_control is a sibling field on a content block, never tokenized as prompt text — a structural fact, not a provider assertion about discard/dedup (avoids the P1/id-190 trap), and it's the identical field already established as PASS_METADATA for manual breakpoints; auto-placement only moves which block carries that metadata. For OpenAI there is no field at all — strictly less added to the wire than the metadata case, which if anything strengthens the pass rather than weakening it. Triage itself concludes "the PASS_METADATA conclusion is probably still directionally fine for both" — its actual complaint is that one telemetrySignal sentence was written to cover two structurally different mechanisms, which is the id-187/id-220 remedy (narrow the scope into the name/signal, don't fail) rather than a mechanism-level FAIL or CONTRACTUAL_ONLY demotion.

refutations.proposedName: Automatic caching, provider-managed (Anthropic: single top-level cache_control breakpoint, auto-searches backward + slides forward; OpenAI: fully implicit longest-prefix hash match, zero client parameter)
refutations.reason:

Triage's two factual claims both check out, and neither one moves the BAR verdict — the questionable flag conflates a documentation/citation defect in the entry with a substantive failure, which it is not.

ANTHROPIC — confirmed verbatim, live, today, from https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching (redirect target of docs.claude.com, raw HTML, not the WebFetch markdown pass):
"How automatic prefix checking works You can use just one cache breakpoint at the end of your static content, and the system will automatically find the longest prefix that a prior request already wrote to the cache."
"How automatic caching works in multi-turn conversations With automatic caching, the cache point moves forward automatically as conversations grow. Each new request caches everything up to the last cacheable block, and previous content is read from cache."
This is exactly the entry's claim: one top-level cache_control flag → provider auto-places/slides the breakpoint. Not stale, not moved.

OPENAI — triage is right that the entry's telemetry signal is Anthropic-only phrasing. Confirmed via raw HTML today from https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching (grepped the raw file, zero hits for "cache_control" anywhere on the page):
"Prompt Caching works automatically for eligible requests, with no code changes required. It is enabled for all recent models, gpt-4o and newer."
"By default, caching is enabled automatically for prompts that are 1,024 tokens or longer... Requests are routed to a machine based on prompt_cache_key, with a hash of the initial prefix of the prompt as a secondary key... Monitor cache reads with cached_tokens."
So: no cache_control field exists in OpenAI's request schema at all — the entry's literal telemetry signal ("a single top-level cache_control flag present in the logged request") would never fire for OpenAI, exactly as triage said.

Where triage's flag overreaches: that telemetry-signal defect is a P5-adjacent citation/precision problem (the entry cites nothing, has no verifiedAgainst date, and its one detection method doesn't generalize across the two providers it names) — not a BAR failure. THE BAR asks only whether the model reads different tokens, a different model answers, or a different amount of thinking happens. For OpenAI that answer is if anything more clearly "no" than for Anthropic: prompt_cache_key/cache routing is explicitly documented as being about which machine serves the request, never part of the model's input content, and nothing is added to the wire by default. Triage itself concedes this ("PASS_METADATA conclusion is probably still directionally fine for both, arguably stronger for OpenAI"). An inapplicable detection recipe for one of two named providers doesn't retroactively make the classification wrong for either provider — it makes the entry's write-up sloppy. Per this register's own established remedy for a merged-mechanism entry (ids 187, 220), the fix is to move the split into the NAME (proposed above) and add per-provider verifiedAgainst citations, not to fail or downgrade a verdict that both the fresh fetch and triage's own analysis support. result.synthesis:
**1. What the passing column is worth.** Of the 69 never-challenged entries, 33 were graded clean on a single triage pass and were never actually attacked — that's "unverified," not "proven." The other 36 were flagged and each hit by two independent refuters. 21 survived both attacks unanimously — the only entries here that are genuinely battle-tested. 9 were overturned by both refuters: 3 are dead outright (ids 38, 124, 138 — FAIL/INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE), and 6 survive only demoted to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY or a narrower rescoped claim (36, 74, 102, 125, 159, 178). 6 more (39, 92, 126, 164, 176, 177) are still contested — one refuter upheld, one overturned, nobody broke the tie. So: 54/69 (78%) hold with no dissent, but only 21/69 (30%) were actually proven under fire; 9/69 (13%) are confirmed wrong as originally graded; 6/69 (9%) are simply unresolved. Rounded in the register's favor, that's "60 pass." Rounded honestly: 54 survive cleanly, and 15 — better than one in five of everything put to the test — do not hold as originally graded.

**2. The most common pattern.** P1 (a documentation sentence doing a structural argument's job — trusting the provider's word about internal discard, dedup, billing, or spend-cap behavior) and P5 (a cited number, issue status, or price that has since moved) dominate, together accounting for most of the 36 flags; P3 (unenforced caller-side conditions) is a distant third; P2 and P4 are rare. That skew says the register's characteristic failure isn't fabrication — nearly every quote checked out verbatim against a live fetch — it's epistemic laundering: real documentation, accurately quoted, silently upgraded from "the provider's word" to "structural proof" without anyone measuring the actual wire. And citations go stale in place: closed-then-fixed issues cited as open, discounts that moved from 75% to 90%, blog posts superseded by the pricing table they once matched.

**3. Attacked and strengthened.** id 152 (streaming-disconnect billing) is the clearest case: the demotion claimed Anthropic's own billing docs were silent on this, and a refuter went and found the actual Help Center page, upgrading the entry from "inferred" to a dated primary-source quote. id 9 and id 175 both survived P4 dependency-skipped challenges because someone read the suspect library's actual source (`filter_value_from_dict`; a real pass-through unit test) instead of trusting the original entry's paraphrase. id 148 got its missing citations traced back and restored from an upstream research file. id 66 (Vaudit) came back with the vendor's own fee structure independently sourced, showing the evidentiary risk sits only in the savings estimate, not the mechanism. Each is now better-sourced than before it was attacked — that's what "survived" should mean, and here it does.

**4. What this audit never checked.** Nothing here involved sending an actual request and reading back the raw response. Every P1 finding — SQS dedup, Bedrock's `clientRequestToken`, capped-spend accounts, refusal billing — stayed at "the provider said so" because nobody drove a real duplicate call, a real capped account, or a real refusal and captured the wire bytes or the invoice line. That is the one test that would settle P1 instead of re-quoting it. Second, the 6 split verdicts were never given a tiebreaker; they sit exactly where they landed, undecided, and this synthesis inherits that gap rather than closing it. Third, none of the roughly twenty proposed corrections — wrong savings percentages, missing `verifiedAgainst` dates, narrowed names — were confirmed as actually written back into the register. This audit produced recommendations, not edits; whether standing-passes.json itself changed is unknown.
